title: Checkpoint: Climate and Weather
objective: After this level you can explain how sunlight, wind, water and mountains combine to make weather and climate.
summary: The Hadley cell ties the chapter together: sunlight lifts air at the Equator, which rains; the dried air sinks near 30 degrees, making deserts, and returns as the trade winds.

cards.headline: Rainforest at the Equator, desert near the tropics. One loop of air does both.
cards.body: You already know the pieces: Level 32's sunshine, Level 33's winds, Level 34's rising and sinking air. Time to snap them together.

cards.headline: Up at the Equator
cards.body: Direct sunlight heats the air near the Equator, and up it goes, like Level 33's hot-air balloon. As it rises it cools and drops its moisture as heavy rain, which is why the Equator is so rainy. The air, now wrung dry, spreads out toward the poles, high in the sky.

cards.headline: Down near 30 degrees
cards.body: Around 30° north and south, that dry air sinks and warms up again. Sinking air blocks clouds from forming, just like on Level 34's leeward slopes, so little rain falls and deserts like the Sahara form. Then the air flows back toward the Equator along the ground, bent by the Coriolis effect. That return flow is the trade winds. Loop closed.

cards.fact: George Hadley proposed this loop in 1735 to explain the trade winds.
cards.context: The loop now carries his name: the Hadley cell. It links nearly everything in this chapter. Sunlight makes the heat, pressure makes the wind, rising air makes the rain, and sinking air makes the deserts.

mascot.line: Sun, wind, rain and desert, all in one loop. That is a whole chapter in a single breath of air.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: Sunlight lifts air at the Equator, where it rains
The dried air sinks near 30°, making deserts
It returns to the Equator as the trade winds
George Hadley proposed the loop in 1735

questions.prompt: Where does the air in a Hadley cell sink back toward the ground?

options.label: Right at the Equator
Around 30° north and south
At the polar circles
options.rationale: The Hadley cell turns back well before that.

options.label: Over the highest mountains
options.rationale: It sinks by latitude, not by mountains.

questions.explanation: The dried-out air sinks around 30° north and south, where it warms and blocks clouds.

questions.prompt: Why is the Equator so rainy?

options.label: Warm, rising air cools and drops its moisture
Sinking air squeezes rain out of the clouds
The trade winds bring rain from the poles
options.rationale: They blow in from about 30°, not from the poles.

options.label: It sits in a rain shadow

questions.explanation: Direct sunlight heats the air, which rises, cools and drops its moisture as heavy rain.

questions.prompt: Which winds from Level 33 carry the Hadley cell's air back to the Equator?

options.label: Monsoon winds
options.rationale: Those reverse by season; the return flow is steady.

options.label: Tornado winds
Winds blowing from the poles
The trade winds

questions.explanation: The air that sank near 30° flows back toward the Equator along the ground, bent by the Coriolis effect: the trade winds.

questions.prompt: Sinking, warming air makes deserts in the Hadley cell. Where did Level 34 show the same effect?

options.label: On the windward side of a mountain
options.rationale: That's where air rises and rains.

options.label: Inside a thunderstorm updraft
options.rationale: Updrafts rise; the dry effect needs sinking air.

options.label: On the leeward side of a mountain range
At the center of a hurricane
options.rationale: Hurricanes are built on rising air.

questions.explanation: On the leeward side of mountains, sinking air warms and its clouds clear, leaving a rain shadow like Death Valley.

questions.prompt: Using Levels 32 and 38: what starts the loop that puts big hot deserts about 15 to 30 degrees from the Equator?

options.label: Cold air sinking at the poles
options.rationale: The Hadley loop starts at the Equator.

options.label: Direct sunlight heating air near the Equator
Mountains lifting air near the tropics
options.rationale: Mountains make rain shadows, not this loop.

options.label: The Moon pulling on the atmosphere
options.rationale: The Sun, not the Moon, drives it.

questions.explanation: Direct sunlight heats the equatorial air, which rises and rains; the dried air then sinks near 30°, where the deserts lie.
